newsitem.title: USA: White House, Congress hope for budget deal.
newsitem.headline: White House, Congress hope for budget deal.

text.p: The White House and Congress Wednesday held out hopes of negotiating a balanced budget, though they warned that deep differences over tax cuts and Medicare spending remained.

President Clinton was scheduled to meet House Democrats Wednesday to hear their concerns about cutting programmes dear to the party's heart -- health care for the elderly and poor, education and the environment. He has scheduled a meeting with Senate Democrats Thursday.
Still, formal bipartisan negotiations were not to resume until late in the week at the earliest and most likely would take place next week.
The president's chief negotiator, Office of Management and Budget Director Frank Raines, told a Senate hearing he hoped for a budget in a few weeks.

"I hope that in the coming weeks, the administration can reach a bipartisan agreement with the Congress to put policies in place this year, which will enable us to reach a balanced budget in 2002," Raines said.

In the Senate, Majority Leader Trent Lott told reporters he felt it was important to strike a deal quickly before factions in each party made so many demands it would be impossible to muster a majority to pass the budget.

"I think that the longer we wait now, the more difficult it is going to be to get an agreement," he said at his regular news conference. Conservative Republican senators said Wednesday they had drawn "a line in the sand" to demand substantial tax cuts and consistently declining federal deficits.

But to reach a deal, Lott said, will require administration movement toward Republicans in key areas. "The president must come off of his continued insistence to spend more, more, more in many categories," he said. Still, he said, the outlook was favourable. "There have been documents passed before me that looked like they are making progress," he said.
"We are still moving ahead as rapidly as we can, this has reached a different stage," Sen. Pete Domenici, the Republican chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, told reporters.
"In the last couple of days there have been new items put on the table," the New Mexico senator said.

A spokeswoman for House Speaker Newt Gingrich said no deadline was being set for conclusion of the talks. But the movement on the budget was being watched closely by financial markets. Reuter reported Tuesday's U.S. Treasuries market was buoyed by hopes for a budget agreement.

The budget is a blueprint for spending and taxes, but does not require the president's signature. Congressional action on separate legislation that will in fact cut taxes, cut social programmes and cut the size of the government is months away and does need the president's approval to become law.

After huddling with Georgia Republican Gingrich and Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, House Majority Leader Dick Armey echoed his Senate colleagues in telling reporters "there were encouraging signs" that an eventual budget deal would be reached with the White House.

Republicans have said the president needs to add about $20 billion to the $100 billion reduction in Medicare spending over the next five years. They have also said tax cuts of $20 billion to $40 billion over his $98 billion through 2002 are necessary.

But the major battle may come in spending for the rest of the government -- the education, environment, parks and other federal agencies -- which Clinton sought to boost next year. Called "non-defence discretionary spending," this money is approved by Congress each year. Disputes over the deep cuts sought by Republicans eager to downsize the government led to two government shutdowns in the last congressional session.

Clinton's chief negotiator, Budget director Frank Raines, said he was sticking with the $100 billion Medicare spending reduction and Senate Democrats have said a tax cut must stay in the "double-digits"-- under $100 billion over five years.
